rounds.text: IRB InvIT Fund trades at an attractive price-to-book ratio of 0.95x, sitting below its book value of ₹ 65.2 at a market price of ₹ 61.8 [E2, E52]. Income-focused investors are well compensated by a substantial dividend yield of 10.70% [E4]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow model values intrinsic worth at ₹ 68 per share, establishing a clear margin of safety above the current market price [E38, E39]. The reverse DCF indicates that today's price implies an earnings growth rate of only 10.7%, which sits below the base case assumption of 12.0% [E40]. Operational fundamentals show immense recent strength with trailing twelve-month compounded sales growth surging by 77% [E16] alongside stellar cash conversion of 3.76x, where operating cash flow of Rs 1,275 Cr for Mar 2026 fully backs reported profits [E30, E31]. Conceded: [E19] compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months is -28%.

Conceded: [E30]. Despite that isolated cash conversion metric, IRB InvIT Fund exhibits severe fundamental weaknesses and escalating financial risk that undermine its valuation. Compounded profit growth over 3 years stands at -5% and has worsened dramatically to -28% over the trailing twelve months [E18, E19]. Operational efficiency is rapidly deteriorating, evidenced by quarterly operating margins tumbling to 70% in September 2026 from 84% in the year-ago quarter, a steep drop of 14 percentage points [E27]. Furthermore, leverage is a major vulnerability as borrowings expanded sharply to ₹ 12,105 Cr in September 2026 from ₹ 9,361 Cr a year earlier, driving the debt-to-equity ratio to 1.12x where debt exceeds net worth [E33, E35]. Return metrics further expose an underperforming asset base, with a 3-year median return on equity stuck at a low 7% and trailing ROCE hovering near a modest 4.03% to 7.0% [E10, E12, E24]. Finally, the business is flagged for a low interest coverage ratio and potential capitalization of interest costs, compounding concerns over earnings quality and structural capital intensity [E54, E58].

Conceded: [E18, E19, E27]. However, the bear's alarm over leverage and borrowings ignores that short-term liquidity is fully comfortable with a current ratio of 2.00x [E34]. While borrowings increased [E35], the company generated substantial operational firepower, posting a massive operating cash flow of Rs 1,275 Cr and free cash flow of Rs 1,000 Cr in March 2026 [E31, E32]. This proves that profits are fully backed by robust cash conversion of 3.76x, directly neutralizing concerns over earnings quality [E30]. Furthermore, the valuation remains deeply attractive: the stock trades at a price-to-book of just 0.95x against a significantly higher sector benchmark of 1.38x, alongside a low price-to-book of 0.68x on key ratios [E2, E7]. Investors are also well-compensated to hold while value is realized, supported by a rich dividend yield of 10.70% [E4]. Finally, a discounted cash flow model explicitly places intrinsic value above the current market price, leaving a clear margin of safety [E38, E39].

Conceded: [E34]. The bull's reliance on cash flow and dividend yield ignores severe structural deterioration in underlying earnings, evidenced by a 3-year compounded profit growth of -5% and a -28% contraction over the trailing twelve months [E18, E19]. Operating margins are collapsing, plunging by 14 percentage points in the September 2026 quarter to 70% from 84% a year prior [E27]. Furthermore, the bull downplays mounting debt risks: total borrowings surged to Rs 12,105 Cr in September 2026 from Rs 9,361 Cr a year earlier, driving debt-to-equity to 1.12x where obligations exceed net worth [E33, E35]. This leverage burden is compounded by explicit warnings that the company has a low interest coverage ratio and may be capitalizing interest costs [E54, E58]. Finally, the claimed valuation safety net is illusory given that multi-year sales growth sits at a meager 1% over three years and 5% over five years, severely lagging broader sector benchmarks [E15, E55].
